items.questionAndWhy: Does the credibility of a fact-checking source change how people interpret a “true” or “fake” label on a health headline?
items.whatTheyDid: In an EEG experiment, 53 participants rated trust in and willingness to share medical headlines before and after labels attributed to more- or less-credible sources. Researchers also examined event-related brain responses.
items.whatTheyFound: Credible sources changed ratings more strongly. “True” labels increased trust and sharing intention only when attributed to a credible source; “fake” labels reduced both regardless of source credibility. No expected FRN/RewP signal emerged. Credible sources produced an early P2-like response, with some P2/P3 variation associated with ratings.
items.whatItMeans: A correction’s source and whether it affirms or refutes a claim can matter differently. The study measures immediate judgments and sharing intentions, not actual sharing or durable belief change. The EEG associations do not uniquely establish the decision mechanism.
items.streamTitle: Fact-check labels depended on source credibility and label direction
items.streamSummary: An EEG study of 53 people found credible-source “true” labels raised trust and sharing intentions, while “fake” labels lowered them from either source. Actual sharing and durable belief change were not tested.
items.attribution: Morozova et al. — Scientific Reports (EEG experiment)

items.questionAndWhy: Is gratitude formed only after seeing a good outcome, or does it update as people learn another person’s intention, action and contribution?
items.whatTheyDid: Across three experiments with six laboratory or online cohorts totaling 547 participants, researchers used an interactive help-and-punishment game and collected gratitude ratings before and after outcomes. They manipulated benevolent intentions and whether help was decisive, irrelevant or harmful.
items.whatTheyFound: Help elicited gratitude before recipients knew the result. Gratitude rose most when effective help made the difference between success and failure. Even irrelevant help could affect ratings through outcome valence. Models using outcome thresholds fitted better than simple continuous prediction-error accounts; some competing explanations remained possible.
items.whatItMeans: Social evaluations can change as causal credit is updated, not just with the final payoff. This offers a testable process model for cooperation and feedback research, but controlled game ratings do not establish later real-world reciprocity or the same dynamics in operational relationships.
items.streamTitle: Gratitude reflected intent, outcome and whether helping made the difference
items.streamSummary: Six cohorts across three experiments found gratitude emerged before final outcomes and changed most when help was decisive. The experiments measured reported emotion in controlled interactions, not lasting cooperative behavior.
items.attribution: Hu et al. — Communications Psychology (three experiments)

items.questionAndWhy: Do unconditional partisan loyalty and a tendency toward conspiratorial explanations help account for unwillingness to include political opponents?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers analyzed a two-wave, diverse US online panel survey and tested associations among obstinate partisanship, conspiracy mentality and political intolerance, including a statistical mediation model.
items.whatTheyFound: Rigid partisan loyalty and conspiracy mentality significantly predicted more intolerant attitudes toward political outgroups. A mediation model was consistent with conspiracy mentality partly accounting for the relationship between obstinate partisanship and intolerance.
items.whatItMeans: Identity commitment and conspiratorial worldviews are distinct candidate correlates of exclusionary political attitudes. Survey-based mediation does not prove a causal pathway, and the study measured attitudes rather than subsequent political exclusion or violence.
items.streamTitle: Conspiracy mentality and rigid partisanship tracked political intolerance
items.streamSummary: A two-wave US panel linked obstinate partisan loyalty and conspiracy mentality to intolerant political attitudes. The mediation model is observational and cannot establish that either factor causes exclusion.
items.attribution: Gil de Zúñiga, Cheng and Scheffauer — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.questionAndWhy: How do a message’s source and content relate to sharing, cognitive expression and emotion as an emergency develops?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers analyzed 68,166 Weibo posts concerning the 2025 Tibet earthquake. They used a time-series vector autoregression model with exogenous variables to examine source characteristics, content cues, collective cognitive-emotional expression and dissemination.
items.whatTheyFound: Early in the observed series, source credibility and activity were associated with less dissemination, while source influence, severity and susceptibility were associated with more. Source effects weakened over time, while content-related associations persisted. Cognitive expressions were more strongly linked to content; emotional expressions to source cues.
items.whatItMeans: Emergency communicators should distinguish source effects from message effects and examine timing rather than rely on a single engagement average. These are modeled associations in one crisis and platform, not causal tests of message design or verified individual cognitive states.
items.streamTitle: Weibo earthquake data showed changing source and content associations with sharing
items.streamSummary: A time-series study of 68,166 Weibo posts found source characteristics mattered more early and content-related cues persisted longer. The results are observational associations, not verified causal effects on sharing.
items.attribution: Lu et al. — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (Weibo time-series analysis)

items.questionAndWhy: How is the Army testing command-and-control integration and information-advantage formations during a multinational exercise?
items.whatTheyDid: An October 29 Army account described Joint Warfighting Assessment 26 within Avenger Triad 26: about 100 modernization-assessment personnel observed an exercise involving roughly 4,000 US and allied participants across four countries. Teams examined corps/theater effects convergence and beta-tested a live experiment-assessment dashboard.
items.whatTheyFound: Army assessors reported that many lessons concerned command-and-control gaps. They examined the role of a Theater Information Advantage Detachment alongside emerging formations and used the dashboard to connect observations across experiments. The report provided no controlled estimate of decision-speed, interoperability or adversary effects.
items.whatItMeans: The useful development is an evaluation architecture that links formation concepts, operational decision requirements and continuous evidence capture. Claims of improved information advantage still need explicit measures and independently assessed exercise outcomes; this is an official account of experimentation, not proof of effectiveness.
items.streamTitle: Army exercise linked information-advantage formations to live assessment
items.streamSummary: Joint Warfighting Assessment 26 assessed theater-level effects and beta-tested a dashboard for experiment evidence during a 4,000-person multinational exercise. The Army did not report controlled decision-quality or operational gains.
items.attribution: Koester — U.S. Army Joint Modernization Command report

items.questionAndWhy: Can automatic evaluators reliably tell whether computer-using AI agents obeyed the full instruction when a long task looks mostly complete?
items.whatTheyDid: The AgentHorizon preprint assembled 1,373 instruction–trajectory pairs from 166 hours of human-recorded computer use across three operating systems. Researchers evaluated 11 judges on long trajectories, including near-miss pairs where a similar but incompatible instruction was substituted.
items.whatTheyFound: The strongest reported judge, GPT-5.5, reached 80.9% balanced accuracy on the main subset. Tool-using evaluation helped some judges but worsened results for certain open-weight models. Judges varied in accepting valid traces and rejecting subtly invalid ones.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX publication and research agents need evidence that every required action occurred, not merely a persuasive final answer or success flag. This benchmark tests computer-use judging, not the truth of a research conclusion; reliability on PSYWERX workflows must be tested separately.
items.streamTitle: AgentHorizon exposed hidden failures in long AI computer-use tasks
items.streamSummary: A 1,373-pair benchmark of long computer-use trajectories found the best tested judge reached 80.9% balanced accuracy. Similar-looking but instruction-incompatible executions remain hard to identify.
items.attribution: Lù et al. — arXiv preprint (AgentHorizon benchmark)

items.questionAndWhy: Can AI agents be evaluated as collaborators with real workers rather than only as autonomous task finishers?
items.whatTheyDid: CollabSkill paired 93 workers with agents on occupationally matched tasks, collecting over 1,500 prompts across 386 work sessions. A Bayesian skill-rating approach tried to separate workers’ and agents’ contributions to results.
items.whatTheyFound: The reported ranking differed from autonomous-agent benchmarks: Claude Code led the tested collaborative setting while Codex led the autonomous comparison. Practical experience was associated with collaboration skill, and hands-on sessions related to changes in reported AI literacy.
items.whatItMeans: A research assistant should be evaluated alongside actual practitioners and for the joint work product, not solely for independent benchmark scores. This preprint is an unusually concrete human-agent evaluation design; it does not establish a universally best model or causal effects of AI experience.
items.streamTitle: Real-worker AI collaboration rankings differed from autonomous-agent rankings
items.streamSummary: CollabSkill analyzed 386 sessions with 93 workers and found agent rankings changed when tested in human collaboration rather than autonomy. Worker experience mattered; generalization beyond the sampled tasks is uncertain.

items.questionAndWhy: Can the Theory of Planned Behavior be made executable over time instead of treating attitudes, norms, control and intentions as static predictors?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers developed a dynamic agent-based formalization of the Theory of Planned Behavior that includes feedback from performed behavior to attitude. Mathematical analysis and model experiments explored how attitude influence and bounded rationality affect collective transitions.
items.whatTheyFound: Within the specified model, varying attitude-influence strength and decision rationality changed whether a population shifted toward adopting a beneficial behavior or rejecting a harmful one. These are modeled transitions under assumed update rules, not observed population changes.
items.whatItMeans: This provides a specific candidate architecture for PSYWERX causal simulations: represent intention formation and post-action feedback separately. It must be calibrated and prospectively checked against people before using the simulated transitions for COA forecasts. Included as underreported model-building work, not a new human finding.
items.streamTitle: Dynamic Theory of Planned Behavior model tested behavior–attitude feedback
items.streamSummary: An agent-based formalization of the Theory of Planned Behavior produced collective shifts under different rationality and attitude-feedback assumptions. It is a theoretical model, not validated human forecasting.
items.attribution: Song et al. — arXiv preprint / IFAC World Congress paper

items.questionAndWhy: When provenance metadata is stripped, which technical methods can reconnect images, audio or video to an authenticated source without creating false matches?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers benchmarked 25 image, seven audio and seven video watermark configurations from 12 methods, plus 35 fingerprinting methods. They used open-licence data, calibrated false-match rates on held-out negatives and evaluated transformed media and adversarial conditions.
items.whatTheyFound: Several watermark detectors produced worrying false alarms on unmarked content; every tested TrustMark error-correcting variant fired on 5.9–15.3% of unmarked images. The best copy detectors found up to 75.5% of transformed images at a pairwise false-match rate of 10^-7. Watermarks and fingerprints failed on different examples, so using both increased coverage.
items.whatItMeans: A concrete information-integrity workflow should test expected watermark payloads, calibrate false matches and use complementary recovery methods rather than treat a detection bit as proof. This is a benchmark under specified transformations, not evidence of universal forgery detection or real-world platform deployment.
items.streamTitle: Provenance benchmark showed complementary watermark and fingerprint failures
items.streamSummary: An open-licence benchmark found some watermark detectors flagged 5.9–15.3% of unmarked images, while strong fingerprint methods recovered many transformed copies. Neither approach alone authenticated all media.
items.attribution: Kazempourradi, Mojtahedi and Mohseni — arXiv preprint (multimedia provenance benchmark)
